prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing neutral-atom clocks to fractional uncertainties near one part in 10^18.

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from the Higgs discovery (B019) to optical lattice clocks (B059). The discovery is a genuine clue from nature in the sense I care about: Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift, Doppler and recoil limits at once, and the clocks have been reproduced and compared in several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) and now resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres. The attribution is compact and no member disputes the two names: the concept and first strontium realisation on one side, the accuracy frontier and many-body clock physics on the other. The overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes is, on reflection, answerable. Those prizes honoured the toolbox (the comb as clockwork, control of single trapped ions); the magic-wavelength lattice is a different physical idea, interrogating very many neutral atoms without systematic shifts, and the citation should rest on that idea alone, not on the comb or on optical clocks in general. The pending redefinition of the second I read as a sign of maturity rather than a reason to wait: metrologists are about to bet the unit of time on this class of devices. I still think the Higgs is the larger discovery of nature, and I do not withdraw that; I move because a prize whose names cannot be defended is a worse prize.
statement.case_against: Priority and distinctness are the real risks. Lemonde, Gill, Bloom, Ludlow, Takamoto and others did real work, and I have not checked the 2003 to 2006 primary record myself, so I rely on the near-unanimous proposal of Katori and Ye and on the committee asking outside reviewers to confirm the boundary between Katori's proposal and first demonstrations and Ye's accuracy work. A sceptic can still say that Ye's credit overlaps with Hall's comb lineage and that the largest payoffs (the redefined second, geodesy, dark-matter searches) are still prospective. Finally, my own earlier worry stands: the Higgs, a finished discovery with a decade of coupling measurements and no prize for the particle itself, goes unrecognised again, and the committee should record that this is a decision about defensible credit and not a judgement that the clocks are scientifically larger.

responses.point: Johansson argued that the Higgs prize would choose collaboration leaders rather than recognise a discovery, since I named Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee and conceded Della Negra is excluded, whereas two names for lattice clocks have no comparable problem.
responses.response: You are right and I now concede the point. In round 1 I treated attribution as a drafting problem; after reading everyone I cannot say what scientific decision distinguishes Virdee from Della Negra, or Gianotti as announcing spokesperson from the ATLAS founders. Any three names would be an administrative reading of two collaborations of thousands. That is the decisive reason for my move. On your question whether my low ranking of B059 rested on overlap alone: it did, together with the prospective payoff, and your answer that the magic-wavelength idea is a new concept rather than a refinement persuades me.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B043) first with Halzen, Karle and Spiering, and says he cannot see a defensible three-name set for the Higgs, while admitting that source-level evidence for TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 is still at modest significance and KM3NeT confirmation is pending.
responses.response: I accept your attribution objection to B019 and it has changed my vote. On IceCube I agree the diffuse flux is secure, but you yourself concede the astrophysical interpretation is not yet independently confirmed at source level and the credit chain through AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND is contested. A prize for opening a window is legitimate, and I keep B043 as an alternative, but I do not think it is more settled than the clocks, where independent groups already agree at the 1e-18 level and the names are not in dispute. If IceCube sources are confirmed by KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD in a few years I would look at it very favourably.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes and whether Lemonde, Gill and Bloom have a claim that a two-name prize would exclude, and he notes that Ye's results are partly built on Hall-lineage comb and cavity-stabilisation work.
responses.response: This answers the chair's first two questions as I see them. The comb and ion-control prizes cover enabling tools; the lattice clock is the combination of a neutral-atom ensemble with a magic wavelength, which is Katori's idea and not Hall's or Wineland's. The citation should therefore say magic-wavelength trapping explicitly and should not mention the comb, which also protects Ye's credit from the double-counting you describe. On priority I agree with you that the primary record must be checked, not assumed, and I would support outside reviewers confirming it. Given your Hall-lineage disclosure I would also welcome the committee noting your view on recusal, though I see no sign it affects the science.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the first lattice-clock demonstrations belong to Katori alone, whether Ye's contribution is an original advance rather than a later, more precise version, and states publicly that the prize is not for the second discoverer who did it better.
responses.response: I share that principle, and it is why the split matters. As I understand the record Katori proposed the scheme and demonstrated it first; Ye's group did more than add decimal places, because reaching 1e-18 required new understanding of blackbody shifts, coherence and collisional physics and turned the clock into a many-body system. I have not verified every date, so I would want that division confirmed against the primary papers before the citation is final. If the record showed that Ye's contribution were only a later, more precise version, I would drop to a one-name or reconsider, but nothing I know suggests that.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B034) as a quantitative prediction followed by experimental discovery of correlated and superconducting states, with the pairing mechanism open, and says he may be undervaluing the clocks because they lie outside his field.
responses.response: I still like prediction followed by confirmation and I do not doubt the phases are real. My reservation is the same as in round 1: eight years, an unresolved pairing mechanism, sample and twist-angle dependence, and Cao and Fatemi, the first experimentalists, outside the credited names, so Jarillo-Herrero's credit is less secure than the theory-plus-experiment pairing suggests. Your own statement that the clock may be undervalued in your field is generous, and I would add that the clock's mechanism is completely understood and the result has been replicated by independent groups. I would revisit B034 in some years if the mechanism settles.

uncertainties: Whether the primary record of 2003 to 2006 supports Katori and Ye alone, or whether Lemonde, Gill, Bloom, Ludlow or Takamoto have a claim that should change the names; I have not verified it and favour outside review.
Whether the committee will accept the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether the citation wording can avoid dependence on the comb.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the second would be wiser than awarding now, though I lean towards treating it as maturity.
Whether the committee will ever settle a defensible three-name set for the Higgs experiments, since I have not changed my view that the particle itself is a major unrecognised discovery.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate. I have no connection to Katori or Ye or to their groups or institutions. I was a CERN fellow in the early 1990s, which has no bearing on ATLAS or CMS (B019), and my supervisor David Gross and my frequent collaborators work in string theory and are not on this shortlist. My earlier first choice, B019, is no longer my preferred part.
